name: Buda Castle Funicular
description: The Buda Castle Funicular, known in Hungarian as the Sikló, climbs a short, steep slope from Adam Clark Square to the castle terrace. First opened in 1870 as a steam-powered line, it was destroyed in the Second World War, rebuilt and reopened in 1986, and is run by BKV as part of city transport.

children.text: The Buda Castle Funicular, known in Hungarian as the Budavári Sikló, connects Adam Clark Square at river level, beside the Chain Bridge, with the castle terrace above. The ride is short: the track is about 95 metres long and climbs roughly 51 metres, with a maximum gradient of 31.75 degrees. Two cars, each carrying up to 24 passengers, run on a double track of standard gauge, and a trip takes about a minute and a half.

The line was an early piece of urban transport engineering. According to the Industrial Heritage Hungary site, Count Ödön Széchenyi proposed a steam-powered funicular to the city authorities in 1867 and received a 40-year concession to build and run it. Ödön Juraszek developed the first plans and Henrik Wolfarth supervised construction from 1869. Building began in July 1868, the first test run took place on 23 October 1869 and the line opened to the public on 2 March 1870. Budapest's funicular is described as the second in Europe, after Lyon's.

A steam engine of about 30 horsepower drove the cars for nearly 75 years, and the line carried more than two million passengers in 1943. Bombing in December 1944 severely damaged it; the cars and terminal buildings were destroyed and the remains were later cleared. The city has owned the line since 1920, and rebuilding was decided in 1965. After 42 years of closure it reopened in 1986. Sources differ on the exact day in 1986, so this guide gives only the year.

Two pedestrian footbridges cross above the track. They existed when the line opened, were removed in 1900 when the castle garden was extended, and were rebuilt to the original design in 1983. Today the funicular is electric and operated by BKV, the Budapest transport company. Its short run makes it both a practical link to the castle terrace and a small piece of Budapest's transport history.
Good to know
Check the BKV or Budapest Info pages for current running days, hours and fares, because they can change with the season and for maintenance.
The lower end is at Adam Clark Square beside the Chain Bridge, the same square as the Buda Castle Tunnel and the Zero Kilometre Stone.
The Buda Castle Tunnel, which opens beside the Chain Bridge, is another landmark in the same square.

children.text: The Buda Castle Funicular provides a direct historic connection between Clark Ádám Square by the Chain Bridge and the Castle Hill palace area. It offers an alternative to climbing the steep slopes on foot.
Its operation and ticketing are separate from ordinary public transport, and services may pause for maintenance.

name: Hungarian Parliament
description: The neo-Gothic seat of Hungary's National Assembly stands on the Pest bank of the Danube. Designed by Imre Steindl and completed in 1904, it is one of Budapest's most recognisable buildings, and its interior can be seen on a guided visit.

children.text: Few buildings define the Budapest riverfront as clearly as the Hungarian Parliament. Its long, lace-like facade, steep spires and central dome stand on the Pest bank of the Danube, facing Buda across the water. The building was designed by Imre Steindl, who won an international competition for the commission. Work began in 1885, the building was inaugurated in 1896, the year of Hungary's millennium celebrations, and it was fully completed in 1904.

The style is Gothic Revival, crowned by a dome in the Renaissance Revival manner. The scale is easiest to grasp in the commonly cited figures: about 268 metres long, 123 metres wide and 96 metres high, with 691 rooms, ten courtyards, 29 staircases and some 242 sculptures inside and out. Construction is said to have used around 40 million bricks and 40 kilograms of gold, and the stained glass and glass mosaics are the work of Miksa Róth.

At the heart of the plan is a sixteen-sided domed hall. On one side lies the chamber of the lower house, where the National Assembly meets; on the other, the former upper house chamber, now used for conferences and ceremonies. Since 2000 the Holy Crown of Hungary has been displayed in the central hall, and it is the main reason many visitors join a guided tour.

Inside, a visit takes you up the ornamental main staircase beneath painted ceilings, past a bust of the architect, and into the ceremonial hall. Visits are arranged through the official visitor centre, which sets the languages, times and prices, so check its website before you plan the day.
Good to know
For the best photographs, stand on the Buda embankment or look from the river; from Kossuth Lajos tér you see only the entrance side.
Guided visits are arranged through the official visitor centre (latogatokozpont.parlament.hu): check languages, dates and ticket conditions there.
Kossuth Lajos tér station (Metro line 2) and tram line 2 stop beside the building.
Nearby: the Shoes on the Danube Bank memorial and St. Stephen's Basilica are both a short walk away.

historyIntro: The Parliament's ornate riverfront silhouette reflects Budapest's emergence as a major European capital at the end of the nineteenth century.

historySections.heading: A purpose-built home for the legislature

children.text: Parliament's building programme began in the 1880s following an architectural competition won by Imre Steindl. The neo-Gothic design combined a dramatic riverside facade with ceremonial chambers and extensive interior decoration.
The legislature held special sessions in the partly completed complex for the 1896 millennium celebrations. The keys to the building were handed over in 1902, and it was fully completed in 1904.

stories.title: An architect who did not live to see his building completed

children.text: Imre Steindl went blind before the building was completed and died in 1902, two years before it was fully finished in 1904.
His design nonetheless became one of the most recognisable symbols of Budapest.

name: Heroes’ Square
description: Heroes' Square is Budapest's great ceremonial space: the Millennium Monument with the seven chieftains and kings of Hungary, flanked by the Museum of Fine Arts and the Műcsarnok at the head of Andrássy Avenue and at the entrance to City Park (Városliget).

children.text: At the end of Andrássy Avenue, Heroes' Square marks the thousandth anniversary of the Magyar settlement of the Carpathian Basin in 896. Construction of the Millennium Monument began in 1896 and was mostly completed by 1900, though the monument was inaugurated in 1905. The square has been officially called Heroes' Square since 1932.

At the centre rises a 36-metre column topped by a bronze statue of the Archangel Gabriel holding the Holy Crown of Hungary and the apostolic double cross, by the sculptor György Zala. It won the Grand Prix at the 1900 Paris Exposition. At the base of the column ride seven mounted figures of the Magyar chieftains, led by Árpád.

Behind the column, a curving two-part colonnade carries statues of Hungarian rulers and leading figures. The line-up has been changed by history: the Habsburg statues were removed during the Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919, rulers' statues were restored in the Horthy era, some were destroyed during the siege of Budapest in World War II, and after the war the Habsburg places were given to leaders of Hungary's struggles for independence, including Imre Thököly, Francis II Rákóczi and Lajos Kossuth in 1954–55.

In front of the column is the Memorial Stone of Heroes, a cenotaph first erected in 1929, removed in 1951 and rebuilt on the same spot in 1956. It is often called the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, but no remains are buried there. The square has also been the stage for national moments: Imre Nagy was reburied here on 16 June 1989.

The square is framed by the Museum of Fine Arts on one side and the Műcsarnok (Hall of Art) on the other, and the municipal park, with its Vajdahunyad Castle copy, begins right behind the monument. Heroes' Square is part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing 'Andrássy Avenue and the Underground' within the wider Budapest site, inscribed in 1987 and extended in 2002.
Good to know
Metro line 1, the Millennium Underground, stops at Hősök tere: it is the quickest way here from the city centre.
Combine it with the Museum of Fine Arts, the Műcsarnok, City Park, Vajdahunyad Castle and the Széchenyi Thermal Bath, which are all within walking distance.
Statues and restoration works change over time: check recent news if a particular monument matters to your visit.

historyIntro: Heroes' Square is a monument built for a national anniversary and then rearranged by every political era that followed, which is why its statues tell as much about the twentieth century as about the Middle Ages.

children.text: The Millennium Monument commemorates the thousandth anniversary of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin, dated to 896. Construction began in 1896 and was mostly completed by 1900, and the monument was inaugurated in 1905. The monument was designed by the architect Albert Schickedanz, and the original sculptural commission went to György Zala, who made the statues of the rulers with several assistants. His bronze Archangel Gabriel, holding the Holy Crown and the apostolic double cross, was installed in 1901 on a 36-metre column, after the work had won the Grand Prix at the 1900 Paris Exposition. The square has officially been called Heroes' Square since 1932.

historySections.heading: Statues that followed the politics of the day

children.text: The colonnade was planned with Habsburg rulers among its figures. During the Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919 the Habsburg statues were removed, the monument was draped in red on 1 May 1919 and a red obelisk replaced the Gabriel statue. The rulers' statues were restored in the Horthy era, and the statues of Maria Theresa and Leopold II were destroyed during the siege of Budapest. After the Second World War the Habsburg places were given to figures from Hungary's struggles for independence, including Imre Thököly, Francis II Rákóczi and Lajos Kossuth, added in 1954–55.

historySections.heading: The Memorial Stone and a national funeral

children.text: In front of the column stands the Memorial Stone of Heroes, a cenotaph first erected in 1929, removed in 1951 and rebuilt on the same spot in 1956. It is often called the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, but no remains are interred there. The square has also been a stage for national moments: on 16 June 1989 Imre Nagy, the prime minister of the 1956 revolution, was reburied here.

stories.title: The archangel, the crown and a royal dream

children.text: A tradition about the first Hungarian king tells of the Archangel Gabriel appearing in a dream and encouraging the creation of a Christian kingdom. The figure atop the Millennium Monument holds the Holy Crown and a double cross in reference to that national and religious story.
The dream belongs to a historical religious tradition, not to a documented eyewitness account. The monument illustrates the story through symbolism.

name: Hungarian State Opera
description: A neo-Renaissance opera house by Miklós Ybl on Andrássy Avenue, opened in 1884. Its horseshoe auditorium, grand staircase, painted ceilings and bronze chandelier were restored in a project completed in 2022, and the company also uses the Erkel Theatre as a second venue.

children.text: The Hungarian State Opera House stands at Andrássy út 22 and was designed by Miklós Ybl, whom one account describes as one of the greatest architects of European historicism. It is a neo-Renaissance building, begun in 1875 and funded by the city of Budapest and Emperor Franz Joseph I. It opened to the public on 27 September 1884 as the Hungarian Royal Opera House. One account says Ybl won the tender that Frigyes Podmaniczky called in 1873.

The facade is meant to show the link between European and Hungarian music. Statues of Ferenc Erkel and Franz Liszt by Alajos Stróbl stand in niches beside the main entrance. Erkel composed the Hungarian national anthem and was the opera house's first music director. Károly Lotz's two sphinxes beside the entrance are made of Carrara marble. The original facade sculptures grew mouldy within a few decades and new ones were made in the 1960s, so the figures seen today are not the first set.

Inside, the horseshoe-shaped auditorium seats around 1,261 people according to Wikipedia. According to Wikipedia, the vast, sweeping main staircase allowed ladies to show off their new gowns. A bronze chandelier weighing about three tonnes, made by craftsmen from Mainz, hangs beneath Károly Lotz's fresco of the Greek gods on Olympus. Murals by Bertalan Székely and Mór Than on the foyer vaults depict the nine Muses, and the boxes beside the royal box carry sculptures representing the four operatic voices. A former smoking room near the artists' entrance holds a gallery of portraits and caricatures of about 600 backstage workers and orchestra musicians, and a rumour says the painters were paid a beer for each.

The house was technically ambitious for its time. A 2014 article notes a hydraulic device for moving the stage and says electric lighting was added from 1895. Gustav Mahler was director of the opera from 1888 to 1891, and Otto Klemperer was music director from 1947 to 1950.

The building has been restored twice in recent decades. A major renovation from 1980 to 1984 ended with a reopening on 27 September 1984, exactly a century after the original opening. A second restoration, lasting nearly five seasons, restored the gold paint and other original decorative surfaces, improved the basement waterproofing and building services, rebuilt the orchestra pit to improve the acoustics and replaced the stage machinery installed in 1984. The house reopened on 12 March 2022. The Opera's second venue is the Erkel Theatre, which opened in 1911 as the Népopera and has been part of the Hungarian State Opera since 1951.
Good to know
Check the official Opera site for the current performance calendar, tours and tickets, and confirm whether your performance is at the Opera House or at the Erkel Theatre.
The Erkel and Liszt statues flanking the main entrance are on the street side, so they can be seen without entering the building.
The house is on Andrássy Avenue, so it pairs naturally with a walk along the avenue.

historyIntro: Budapest's Hungarian State Opera is both a working performance venue and a monument to the city's nineteenth-century cultural ambitions.

historySections.heading: A palace for a growing capital

children.text: The Neo-Renaissance opera house was designed by Miklós Ybl and opened on 27 September 1884. Its position on Andrássy Avenue helped establish the new boulevard as a showcase of modern Budapest. It gave the opera company a dedicated home; until then opera had been staged at the National Theatre alongside drama.

Painters, sculptors and craftspeople contributed to its celebrated interiors. Károly Lotz's painted ceiling and the ceremonial staircase are as much part of the experience as the stage. A major restoration culminated in the venue's reopening in 2022.

stories.title: An opening night the crowd could not resist

children.text: The Opera House's own account recalls spectators pushing past guards on the opening day in 1884, eager to see the new building. The excitement became part of the institution's history.
This is an anecdote documented by the opera company, not a local ghost legend.
